transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Since my wife and I separated, I’ve felt this heavy, empty mood that I can’t shake, even when I’m at the library or around art. It has just been hanging over me, and my niece really thought I should come in and talk to someone.
How long has this low mood been bothering you, and did it start immediately after your separation?

This heavy, empty feeling has been with me steadily for about three months now. It started right when the separation became official and I moved into my own apartment. It's just been a constant weight ever since.
Besides this heavy, empty mood, have you been experiencing other changes, such as significant shifts in your appetite, sleep patterns, energy levels, or feelings of worthlessness?

Yes, food tastes like cardboard lately so I barely eat, and I lie awake for hours before waking up exhausted at 4 AM. My body also feels like it's moving through molasses, making even simple tasks at the library take forever. I don't really feel worthless, just incredibly empty and slowed down.

Do you find that your low mood and lack of motivation are specifically tied to thoughts about the separation, or do you feel this same persistent heaviness even when you are not thinking about your wife or the divorce?

The heavy, hollow feeling is pretty much constant throughout the day, even when I'm trying to focus on shelving books or looking at art. But it is deeply tied to the separation, because almost everything I see reminds me of my wife and the life we used to have. Even when I try to rest, my mind just loops right back to the divorce.

Do you feel that your current symptoms, like the changes in your appetite and sleep, are primarily a reaction to the stress of the separation, or do you feel that this low state has taken on a life of its own, independent of the divorce?

It feels like a combination of both. The separation was definitely the major trigger that started me looping over the divorce and losing my appetite, but looking back, these cycles of dragging lows and revved-up highs have actually been happening for many years. The breakup has just magnified them and made this current low feel like it has taken over completely.

You mentioned experiencing cycles of revved-up highs in the past; during those times, did you feel unusually energetic, need much less sleep than usual, or find yourself taking on many new projects or risky activities?

Yes, during those high periods I felt incredibly wired and energetic, often sleeping only three or four hours a night but waking up buzzing and ready to go. I would suddenly throw myself into multiple projects at once, staying up late reorganizing my art supplies or drafting plans for new library procedures and community workshops. It felt like I had this restless drive to fix everything in my life in one big, excited push.

During those periods of feeling unusually wired and productive, did you ever find that your behavior became so impulsive or out of character that it caused significant problems at work or in your relationships, or did you feel you were still generally able to function?

During those high-energy times, I was still able to function and actually felt overly productive, starting lots of library projects and working on art late into the night. I might have been a bit snappish or talked too fast, but it never caused any major crises. The real problems, like calling out sick and letting my work pile up, have only happened during these recent low periods.
